performers: BBC Symphony Orchestra; Ralph Vaughan Williams
intro: The composer conducts the BBC Symphony Orchestra in the first movement of his Fourth Symphony, which opens on a grinding semitone clash. The recording was made at Abbey Road in October 1937, two years after the première.

sections.label: A · Fortissimo opening and two themes
Coda · Pianissimo, in a major key

cues.title: Opening semitone clash
cues.text: The symphony opens at once with a fortissimo clash of a semitone. Two principal themes are drawn from it and recur throughout the work.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s note for Hyperion (CDA68280): the symphony “opens with a grinding semitonal fortissimo clash, from which emerge two principal themes”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/68280-B.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four-note figure
cues.text: A four-note figure runs through much of the symphony. Vaughan Williams varies it many times.
cues.evidence: Matthew-Walker’s note: “the all-pervasive four-note figure that inhabits much of the work” and its “seemingly limitless variation”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/68280-B.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paragraph in The Times
cues.text: Ursula Vaughan Williams traced the symphony to a newspaper paragraph in The Times that described an imagined symphony. Her husband reacted at breakfast with “il faut je compose cela”.
cues.evidence: Ursula Vaughan Williams’s biography as quoted in Matthew-Walker’s Hyperion note: “So, without any philosophical, prophetic or political germ, No 4 took its life from a paragraph in The Times.” https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/68280-B.pdf

cues.title: Counterpoint in both themes
cues.text: The two themes are treated in counterpoint virtually throughout the movement, within a compact structure.
cues.evidence: Matthew-Walker’s note: “Virtually throughout they are treated to the composer’s complete mastery of contrapuntal devices” within “inherently compact structures”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/68280-B.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Queen’s Hall, 1935
cues.text: The symphony was first played at Queen’s Hall on 10 April 1935 by the recently formed BBC Symphony Orchestra under Adrian Boult. Vaughan Williams dedicated it to Arnold Bax.
cues.evidence: Matthew-Walker’s note for Hyperion: première at Queen’s Hall on 10 April 1935, BBC Symphony Orchestra, Adrian Boult; dedicated to Sir Arnold Bax. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/68280-B.pdf

cues.title: Recording, Abbey Road, 1937
cues.text: Vaughan Williams conducted this recording with the BBC Symphony Orchestra in Studio 1 at Abbey Road on 11 October 1937. HMV issued the symphony on 78-rpm discs.
cues.evidence: Discogs release 6684057 (EMI, 1987) gives the session as No. 1 Studio, Abbey Road, 11 October 1937, and the HMV 78 numbers; classical-music.com places the session in Abbey Road Studio 1 in October 1937. https://www.discogs.com/release/6684057

cues.title: Vaughan Williams on the symphony’s origins
cues.text: Vaughan Williams always denied that the symphony was a reaction to events in Europe. He could point to other recent works with passages of similar power and conflict, among them the oratorio Sancta civitas, the masque for dancing Job and the piano concerto.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s note for Hyperion (CDA68280): Vaughan Williams denied that the symphony was a reaction to contemporary events and could point to Sancta civitas, Job and the piano concerto, “all of which contain passages of similar power and conflict”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/68280-B.pdf

cues.title: Vaughan Williams on the symphony
cues.text: Vaughan Williams rejected any reading of the symphony as a picture of events outside the music. He said he wrote it “simply because it occurred to me like this. I can’t explain why…”
cues.evidence: Ralph Vaughan Williams Society, “Achievements and Recognition”, which quotes the composer’s own statement on the Fourth Symphony. https://www.rvwsociety.com/achievements

cues.title: Coda, pianissimo, major key
cues.text: The movement ends with a pianissimo coda in a soft major key. Robert Matthew-Walker wrote that here the Pastoral Symphony’s layered harmony is put to a very different expressive use.
cues.evidence: Matthew-Walker’s note: “the pianissimo coda to the first movement, wherein the ‘triplanar harmony’ of the ‘Pastoral’ is put to quite different expressive use by way of a soft major key”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/68280-B.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: BBC Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Ralph Vaughan Williams (conductor)
fields.note: Both the Archive item and the EMI reissue notes credit the composer as conductor. Individual players are not identified.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Complete first movement of the orchestral symphony
fields.note: The Archive item lists the four movements and splits the set into three files without saying which file holds which movement. The first file runs 8 min 2 s and ends in a quiet close that matches Hyperion’s description of the first movement’s pianissimo coda.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Archive item writes the date as 11-10-1937; the EMI reissue notes give 11th October 1937.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The EMI reissue notes name No. 1 Studio, Abbey Road; BBC Music Magazine places the session in Abbey Road Studio 1.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Archive item catalogues the set as DB 8406–9 (automatic coupling); the EMI reissue notes give DB 3367–3370 as the original 78s. They probably label the same performances in two side sequences, but that is not established here.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The Archive description lists the takes; the EMI notes list the same matrix numbers. Which sides make up the first file is not stated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item is filed in that collection; no transfer engineer is named in the description.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive upload date (13 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: FLAC, Ogg Vorbis and variable-bitrate MP3 derivatives, in three segments (a first file, a second, and a third joining the remaining two discs).
fields.note: Equalisation, speed correction and noise reduction are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Vaughan Williams’s copyright in the music runs to the end of 2028 in the UK and EU.
fields.note: The Vaughan Williams Foundation gives 2028 as the year copyright in his music expires. Composition rights are separate from the recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: commercial issue in 1938, before 1963
fields.note: The EMI reissue notes date the original HMV 78s “℗ 1938”. The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule then applies: the former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is not United States or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

composer.died: 26 August 1958, Hanover Terrace, Regent’s Park, London
composer.epithet: Collector of an Essex folk song in 1903, editor of the English Hymnal, and the man who brought a Tudor psalm tune into the concert hall.

Composer, folk-song collector, hymn-book editor, teacher and conductor; Leith Hill Musical Festival, 1905–53

Nine symphonies, operas, a masque for dancing, choral works, songs, hymn tunes, film scores and music for amateurs

quote.text: In the next world, I shan’t be doing music, with all the striving and disappointments. I shall be being it.
quote.source: Vaughan Williams to Sylvia Townsend Warner, about a fortnight before his death in August 1958, as she recorded it in a letter

composer.background:
On 9 February 1875 Arthur Vaughan Williams, vicar of All Saints, Down Ampney, died after a brief illness. His third child, Ralph, born in the vicarage on 12 October 1872, was two. His widow Margaret, a Wedgwood, took the children to her family’s house at Leith Hill Place in Surrey. Aunt Sophy gave the boy piano lessons, and at six he wrote a piece called The Robin’s Nest. He went to Charterhouse in 1887 and to the Royal College of Music in 1890, where Hubert Parry taught him composition; in 1892 he went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, to read history as well as music.

On 9 October 1897, three days before his twenty-fifth birthday, he married Adeline Fisher at All Saints, Hove. She was a cellist and pianist, and Virginia Woolf was her first cousin. After a brief spell of study with Max Bruch in Berlin he returned to his post as organist at St Barnabas, South Lambeth. He had held the post since 1895 and disliked it, and he gave it up in 1899.
